name: Herschel Island Eskimo Trade Jargon
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct trade pidgin; only known material is Stefansson 1909 wordlist, no phonology/stress description found

sources.citation: van der Voort, Hein. 2013. Eskimo Pidgin (survey chapter 76). In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures Online / The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages vol. III. Leipzig: MPI-EVA. https://apics-online.info/surveys/76
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 4 Phonology: 'Stefánsson indicates stress by an apostrophe following the stressed syllable, and hyphens are used to separate syllables, as in sī’-la ‘weather’' and 'In Eskimo proper, phoneme length and stress are unrelated, and the notation of length in the Pidgin sources seems independent of stress notation too.' No statement of where stress falls; later remarks that intonation probably carried illocutionary distinctions.

sources.citation: van der Voort, Hein. 2013. Eskimo Pidgin structure dataset. APiCS Online contribution 76. https://apics-online.info/contributions/76

sources.note: Consonant and vowel inventories only; APiCS has no word-stress feature. Default lect stated to be the Herschel Island Trade Jargon, 'the best documented Eskimo Pidgin known so far'. Sources listed: Faber 1916, Ray 1885, Stefánsson 1909, Wurm 1992, van der Voort 1997.

sources.note: Travel narrative in Fraktur (archive.org untereskimosundw00fabe, Getty scan); scanned text layer is largely garbled. The Herschelinsel chapters are locatable but no jargon phonology or accent discussion could be found; not a linguistic description.

sources.citation: Stefánsson, Vilhjálmur. 1909. The Eskimo Trade Jargon of Herschel Island. American Anthropologist n.s. 11(2): 217-232.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 222, preface to the vocabulary: only a notation statement (Powell's system; minor accent ' and major accent " when a word has two accents) plus a disclaimer that accent and syllabification are the author's own pronunciation, unverified with a Mackenzie speaker. Every headword in the vocabulary (pp. 222-232) carries a stress mark, but no rule of placement is given; my own tally of the marked headwords shows no fixed position (2-syll: 38 initial / 2 final; 3-syll: 23 initial / 23 second / 1 third; 4-syll: 3/2/6).
